newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- FEB 19.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- FEB 19.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:
KATHIMERINI

--The expected further fall in inflation in February (from 6.8 percent in January to 6.5) is expected to give a further push to falling interest rates. Sources say the National Bank of Greece will proceed to a significant reduction in lending rates next week, taking them to below 14.75 percent.

--A three-member committee has recommended wide-reaching changes to the operation of the Greek Post Offices (ELTA), including closures of a number of ELTA's 900 branches, wage adjustments and tariff increases.

--Private schools will be fined if they overcharge parents for tutorial fees, according to a new amendment to be submitted to Parliament today. The fines will range from 50,000-500,000 drachmas per student.

--The controversial amendment on transferring pension funds' reserves to the Bank of Greece resubmitted to Parliament yesterday has been clarified but remains in principle the same. The changes, however, came with the General Confederation of Workers of Greece's (GSEE) blessing.
IMERISIA

--The reason behind the fuss over the pension funds' amendment was who would control the management of cpaital amounting to 2.7 trillion drachmas. The national economy ministry hoped to create a "common capital" which would bring in high returns with the Bank of Greece investing in primary and secondary markets.

--The current accounts balance was in the red to the tune of about four billion dollars in the period January-October 1996, according to the central bank, due in part to the deficit in the trade balance.

--The increased demand for loans may create problems in Greek banks due to a lack of the appropriate infrastructure and risk evaluation systems, Standard & Poor said yesterday in their ratings of Greek banks.
KERDOS

--A European Commmision committee monitoring progress in the Second Community Framework is expected to approve new rules which will allow the transfer of Community funds from projects that have stalled and are not progressing to those in need of funds and able to absorb with satisfactory rates.
--Euromedica will proceed to a share capital increase of 1.2 billion drachmas to be used for new investments and buyouts of companies active in the health field.

--The Supreme Labour Council will discuss the issue of shop trading hours at its session today. If it is approved by the Council the new proposal must still pass through the approval of the national economy and finance and development ministries, who have expressed their opposition to a return to restrictions on trading hours.
EXPRESS
--The dollar reached a record high against the drachma yesterday before closing at 266.54 drachmas, up 0.55 percent over the previous day's fixing.

--Reports have Prime Minister Costas Simitis meeting with farmers of the Thessaly Coordinating Committee next Wednesday, the first time since farmers' began their protests on national roads and rail links last December.
NAFTEMBORIKI

--The Commission is examining how to relax conditions in the labour market to better deal with world competition. Shrinking European productivity and falling employment rates dictates the reappraisal of the organisation of labour and functioning of companies.

--Although 42 Northern Greek firms are suitable candidates for listing on the Athens bourse, 13 are hesitant about the move, saying their planned investments are covered in any case by development laws and economic support from the Community. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
